title: BUG: CLI table text is unreadable on dark terminal themes.

goal.value:
BUG: CLI table text is unreadable on dark terminal themes.

SYMPTOM
Secondary text in `fabro` CLI tables is hardcoded to `Color::Ansi256(8)` ("bright
black" — a fixed dark grey from the palette). That assumes a light terminal
background; on a dark theme it renders nearly invisible against the background.
Reproduced by the user with `fabro workflow list`, where the DESCRIPTION column
is unreadable.

LOCATIONS — 10 occurrences in 4 files, all under
lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/
  runs/list.rs         6  (lines 128, 138, 148, 178, 184, 185)
  model.rs             2  (lines 135, 138)
  workflow/list.rs     1  (line 113)
  run/checkpoints.rs   1  (line 93)

runs/list.rs is the worst case: line 178 uses Ansi256(8) as a *status* color and
line 184 suppresses bold for it, so a run status is conveyed entirely by a color
the user cannot see. This is not purely cosmetic.

SUSPECTED CAUSE
An absolute palette index is used where a terminal-relative attribute belongs.
The codebase already has the right primitive: `fabro_util::terminal::Styles::dim`
= `Style::new().dim()` at lib/foundation/fabro-util/src/terminal.rs:28. It emits
SGR 2 (faint) against the terminal's own foreground, so it adapts to the theme.
workflow/list.rs already uses `styles.dim` for the section path in
`print_section` — the table cells in the same file just don't.

OPEN QUESTION — resolve this before choosing the fix
Does cli-table 0.5's `CellStruct` expose a faint/dim attribute the way it exposes
`.bold(bool)`? Check the actual crate source in the cargo registry rather than
guessing. Three ways it can go:
  a) If CellStruct has a faint/dim attribute, use it. Cleanest.
  b) Otherwise pre-apply the dim style to the string before `.cell()`. Risk:
     cli-table's column width measurement may count the embedded ANSI escape
     codes and mis-align the table. Verify alignment if taking this path.
  c) As a last resort pick a mid-tone color readable on both light and dark
     backgrounds — but this still absolutizes what should be relative.

Note all styling here already goes through the `use_color` flag via
`color_if()`, so the no-color path is unaffected either way.

CONTRIBUTION PATH
Per CONTRIBUTING.md this qualifies as a "bug fix / small improvement" — send a
PR directly, no issue needed. The `origin` remote is the fork
carllelandtaylor/fabro; `upstream` is fabro-sh/fabro and its push URL is
DISABLED, so push branches to `origin` only. Branch from main and open the PR
against fabro-sh/fabro main, e.g.

  gh pr create --repo fabro-sh/fabro --base main --head carllelandtaylor:<branch>

REQUIRED CHECKS (CONTRIBUTING.md's list is stale relative to CI — use these)
  cargo nextest run --workspace
  cargo +nightly-2026-04-14 fmt --check --all
  cargo +nightly-2026-04-14 clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
The pinned nightly matters: stable rustfmt will not match CI.

VERIFICATION
No existing test covers this. Add one asserting the faint attribute (or whatever
the chosen mechanism emits) so this cannot regress. Manually verify the rendered
output against both a light and a dark terminal profile.

prompt.String:
Final validation failed. Fix the issues so the plan's Test Plan passes.

Read the failing output carefully and address the actual cause. Prefer folding each fix into the existing commit it belongs to rather than piling corrections on the end of the stack — the commit stage that follows handles that placement. Stay within the plan's scope.

If the failure has a documented fallback in the plan that has not been tried yet, try it before writing your own fix.

Report what failed, what you changed to fix it, and which commit each fix belongs in.

Create the pull request, or update the existing one in place. Start with `gh pr view --json number,url,state 2>/dev/null`.

If a PR exists and its state is OPEN, take the UPDATE path. If a PR exists and its state is MERGED, ignore it and take the CREATE path — that PR is no longer active. If a PR exists and its state is CLOSED, ask the developer whether to reopen it with `gh pr reopen <number>`, create a new one, or stop. If no PR exists, take the CREATE path.

UPDATE PATH. Never regenerate the body from scratch: the developer may have added sections, screenshots, Loom links, reviewer notes or rewordings that a wholesale replacement would destroy. Do it in a single pass — fetch once, edit once, and do not re-read afterwards to verify. Fetch the current body once with `gh pr view <number> --json title,body`, treat it as the source of truth, and apply the minimum set of edits that make it reflect the current branch state: correct stale information in place, add genuinely new information to the most appropriate existing section, and remove or revise only the specific sentences or bullets that are no longer true. Leave everything else verbatim, including developer-added sections and inline additions; when unsure whether something is stale, keep it. Treat `## Screenshots` under the same rule: if this run captured screenshots and the body has no Screenshots section, add one in the captured form; if a Screenshots section already exists, refresh only its directory pointer and file list to match the currently committed screenshots; if the change is non-visual, leave the body's Screenshots handling untouched. On the update path do NOT insert or modify any `Resolves #N` line and do NOT set a Project Status — that is handled by other automation. Apply everything with a single `gh pr edit <number> --body "..."`.

CREATE PATH. Before running `gh pr create`, check for an active Issue:

    if facto-helper.sh tracker.exists 2>/dev/null; then ISSUE_NUMBER="$(facto-helper.sh current-issue 2>/dev/null)" || ISSUE_NUMBER=""; fi

If `$ISSUE_NUMBER` is set, build the PR-link line by substituting `{issue}` into `facto-helper.sh tracker.field pr_link_format` — default `Resolves #{issue}`, giving `Resolves #123` — and insert it as the second line of the `## Summary` section, immediately after the one-line summary. If `tracker.exists` fails or `current-issue` returns nothing, skip the link entirely.

Build the body from the PR body template at [facto] claude/skills/pr/pr-body-template.md, which defines every section — Summary, Reason for change, What changed, Screenshots, Notable technical choices, Verification — and the footer. Keep the PR title short and in conventional commit format such as `feat:`, `fix:` or `refactor:`, under 70 characters. Fill Reason for change from the reason established earlier in this run. Fill `## Screenshots` from the outcome of the capture step: when capture succeeded use the pointer form, building the directory link from `REPO_SLUG="$(gh repo view --json nameWithOwner -q .nameWithOwner)"`, `BRANCH="$(git branch --show-current)"` and `REL="$(realpath --relative-to="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" "$SHOTS_DIR")"` into `https://github.com/$REPO_SLUG/tree/$BRANCH/$REL`, with one bullet per committed file labelled by screen or state and by before or after; when capture failed use the placeholder form, keeping the unchecked `- [ ] Attach screenshots before merging` item and quoting the specific recorded reason; when the change is non-visual omit the `## Screenshots` section entirely.

Every Manual verification step must describe something that could fail even if every file in the diff is exactly as shown — running a command, starting a dev server and exercising a path, checking a CI run's outcome, parsing a config with a real tool. Do NOT write steps that merely verify a file exists, that content is present, or that a line was deleted; the diff already proves those. `npx playwright test foo.spec.ts` is acceptable, `confirm file X exists` is not; `start dev server, click X, expect Y` is acceptable, `verify section Y is present` is not. Verification steps must be specific enough for someone unfamiliar with the change to follow them. For documentation-only, comment-only, gitignore or pure-config changes with no executable behavior, replace the numbered list with `N/A — documentation-only change; diff review is sufficient.` rather than fabricating steps. End the body with `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`.

prompt.String:
Decide where each change belongs. Do not commit anything in this step.

The base ref and the current commit stack were printed by the assess step. For every changed file — and for every hunk separately when a single file carries changes belonging to different commits — pick exactly one destination:

1. MOST RECENT COMMIT: the change extends or fixes work done in HEAD.
2. AN EARLIER COMMIT: the change extends or fixes work done in a specific prior commit in the stack. Record that commit's hash.
3. NET-NEW: the change is unrelated to every existing commit in the stack and needs its own new commit.

Gather evidence before deciding. Run `git log <base>..HEAD -- <file>` for each changed file, and read the existing commit messages and their diffs (`git show <hash>`). Attribute on what the commits actually did, not on filename similarity.

Output an explicit attribution table: file (or hunk) -> destination -> the evidence that justifies it. Group the net-new changes and note, for each group, whether it should be one commit or several.

Fill in the frames and bands. The board is a vertical stack of bands (rows of frames); inside each frame the dashed .design-slot is the region you replace with real design — replace its contents only, never the device chrome. The template documents itself at the point where you fill it, so open the copy and follow the inline comments: each band's header comment says what that band is for and when to duplicate or remove it, the top-of-file comment lists which frame type goes with which platform, and the Appendix band shows every frame type — delete the Appendix band when you are done. Hold three things across the whole file. Scope: design only the screens the feature touches, never the whole app. Implementability: do not use presentation the target platform cannot build, for example a CSS effect Jetpack Compose cannot reproduce; the mock must be buildable as shown. Completeness: every flow the caller supplied gets its own band running from entry to completion — a flow with no band is a gap, not a simplification. Treat the caller's flow list as given, the same way <dest-dir> is given. Within a flow band, every step is a full-screen frame, an overlay step is that same full screen with the overlay drawn over it, and each connector between steps carries the action that triggers the transition; the band's header comment in the template has the full detail on step granularity and duplication.

Report what this run actually did, using only what happened in the steps above. Do not invent a PR, a commit, or a URL.

If the context step reported that there was nothing to put in a PR, say `Nothing new to put in a PR` and stop there.

Otherwise report, in this order: whether the pull request was CREATED or UPDATED; the PR URL; the PR title; a one-line summary of what the PR covers; and, if any commit work happened, one line per commit that was added or amended — for example `amended into "Add webhook retry"` for a folded-in error handling fix, or `new commit "Fix lint errors"` for addressed eslint warnings. Note the screenshot outcome in one line: the screenshots committed, the reason capture was not possible, or that the change was non-visual. Finally note anything that warned rather than failed, such as a Project Status write that did not go through.

Apply the attribution decided in the previous step. Process the groups strictly in this order: earlier commits first, then the most recent commit, then net-new.

EARLIER-COMMIT CHANGES
    git add <files>
    git commit --fixup=<target-commit-hash>
Create every fixup commit first. When they all exist, squash them in a single pass:
    GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash <base>
If the rebase stops on a conflict, resolve it, `git add` the resolved files, and `git rebase --continue`. Never leave a rebase in progress.

MOST-RECENT-COMMIT CHANGES
    git add <files>
    git commit --amend --no-edit

NET-NEW CHANGES
    git add <files>
    git commit -m <message>

Commit message rules for every new commit. Subject line: imperative mood, no trailing period, describing what the change does. The body must include a Context line saying why this change exists — and when the change introduces a new library, API, or service, what it is and why it was chosen. Add a Verification section when it is meaningful, split into an `Automated:` part listing the exact commands and a `Manual:` part with numbered steps and their expected results. Omit the Verification section entirely for changes that are trivially correct: documentation, comments, or config with no behavioral effect. Keep each body to 2-5 lines — enough for a developer reading `git log` to understand the change without opening the diff. Use the commit message the caller supplied if there is one; otherwise write it yourself.

prompt.String:
Choose between the direct path and the escalated path for the fix approach you just proposed. Escalation is purely about heavier tooling for a bigger change — it is never a request for developer review, and either path runs autonomously to completion.

ESCALATE if ANY of these holds: the fix touches more than about two files, or touches shared or core logic that many things depend on; it introduces a new abstraction or interface; it requires a schema, API or migration change; or it is otherwise large or multi-step.

Otherwise the fix is small and localized, and takes the DIRECT path.

End this stage as SUCCEEDED if the checklist says escalate. End this stage as FAILED if the fix is small and localized and takes the direct path. State which checklist item triggered escalation, or state that none did, so the choice is auditable.

You observed the bug. Both goals must be met before you finish: confirm it reproduces AND log a repeatable sequence. Reduce the path to the minimal precise repeatable sequence by dropping every step that is not required to trigger the bug — re-run after each removal to check the symptom still appears. Record, exactly: PRECONDITIONS AND DATA — required state, fixtures, environment, accounts; ORDERED ACTIONS — the exact numbered steps, with the precise input, click target or command at each; OBSERVED (WRONG) RESULT versus EXPECTED RESULT. Capture evidence that shows the wrong behavior: a screenshot, a log excerpt, command output, or a response body. Then re-run the minimal sequence once more to confirm it reliably reproduces. If it only reproduces intermittently, note that and the observed frequency.

Measure values from the running app rather than estimating them, so the mock matches it rather than approximates it. DEVICE PROFILE: capture the surface's pixel resolution and density, derive the logical size and the device scale factor (dsf), set the frame to that logical size, and adopt 1 CSS px == 1 dp/pt so measured positions map directly into the mock; this replaces the template's default frame dimensions and its generic status bar. Android: adb shell wm size for px and adb shell wm density for dpi, then dsf = dpi/160 and logical = px / dsf. iOS: point size times scale (@2x or @3x), dsf = scale. Web: CSS px directly, dsf = 1 or the device-pixel-ratio you target. Size the frame by setting its CSS variable to the measured logical viewport — --screen-width and --screen-height on a .phone-screen, --frame-width on a .browser. .phone-screen, .browser and .browser-page are template-owned class names: set the variable, never redeclare the class in a separate stylesheet, because the template's frame rules are inlined after any linked CSS and a redeclared width silently loses, which can clip the page. GEOMETRY: read element bounds from the live accessibility or DOM tree, not from the screenshot — adb shell uiautomator dump on Android (Compose exposes semantics bounds in px, divide by dsf for dp), the view or accessibility hierarchy on iOS, getBoundingClientRect() on web. COLORS: take the surface's tokens from source — design-system.md if it has one, otherwise the theme file the code actually uses such as globals.css or a platform theme — and sample the screenshot at known points to confirm. Sampling catches what reading source misses: elevation tints and alpha composites, where a 50-percent-alpha foreground over a variant surface renders as neither token's hex. When the surface has no token reference at all, the sampled values are the source of truth. FONTS: copy the app's actual bundled font files into assets/ and @font-face them, because a substitute webfont changes glyph metrics and shifts alignment. OS CHROME IS NOT THE APP: reproduce the status bar and the gesture or home indicator approximately, and treat them as out of scope when judging fidelity.

prompt.String:
Capture screenshots of any visual change on this branch. This whole step is autonomous — never ask the developer, and never let a capture failure abort the PR.

FIRST, judge on your own whether the changes in this PR could plausibly affect the UI or UX that a person sees or interacts with. Reason about what the change actually does; do not rely on a checklist, a file-extension list, or any other heuristic. If the change could not affect the UI or UX, capture nothing, record that the change is non-visual, and finish this step — no Screenshots section will go into the PR body.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL, delegate the capture work to a subagent so the heavy image tokens stay out of this workflow's context; the subagent must return only the list of screenshot paths and their labels, never the images themselves. The subagent does the following.

1. Resolve the directory: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir)/screenshots"`. If `facto-helper.sh task-dir` fails because you are not in a task worktree, pass a short kebab-case slug instead: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir "<slug>")/screenshots"`. Then `mkdir -p "$SHOTS_DIR"`.
2. Remove stale screenshots from earlier runs so the directory always reflects the current app: `git rm -q "$SHOTS_DIR"/* 2>/dev/null || true`.
3. Bring up the app and capture the after-state of every distinct surface the change affects, with no cap on how many. Prefer, in this order: a project-specific run skill or documented run instructions; the built-in run and verify skills; for web UIs the Playwright tools, navigating to the running app and taking screenshots; for native mobile, booting or attaching an emulator or simulator, launching the app and navigating to the affected screens. Save each capture into `$SHOTS_DIR` under a descriptive labelled filename such as `dashboard-after.png`.
4. Best-effort before-state: when the change modifies an existing screen rather than adding a brand-new one, and the base version is cheaply runnable, add a worktree at the merge base with `git worktree add <tmp> "$(git merge-base main HEAD)"`, run that version, capture the same surfaces into `$SHOTS_DIR` as `*-before.png`, then remove the worktree with `git worktree remove <tmp> --force`. For brand-new screens capture after-only. If running the base version is impractical because of an expensive rebuild or missing services, skip the before-state and note that.
5. Stage ONLY `$SHOTS_DIR` — never `git add -A`. The next step commits what you staged.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL BUT NO VIABLE WAY TO RUN THE APP AND CAPTURE EXISTS, capture nothing and record the specific reason, for example 'no emulator available' or 'app build failed'. The PR body will then carry the placeholder form of the Screenshots section quoting that reason.

Never wrap `git` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper. Report exactly one of: the committed-screenshot paths with their labels; the specific capture-failure reason; or that the change is non-visual.

Decide which branch this pull request is opened from. Never ask the developer for a branch name.

If `git branch --show-current` already reports a non-main branch such as `feat/foo` or `fix/bar`, use it as the PR branch and do nothing else in this step.

If you are on `main` or `master`, derive a branch name yourself and create it. Choose the PREFIX from the conventional-commit type of the first commit ahead of main — `feat/`, `fix/`, `chore/`, `docs/`, `refactor/`, `test/` — and default to `chore/` when the first subject is not in conventional-commit form. Choose the SLUG as a short kebab-case description of three to five words drawn from keywords common to the commit subjects ahead of main; if there are no commits yet, slugify from the staged and unstaged file paths or a short summary of the working-tree diff. For example, commits `feat(auth): add X` and `feat(auth): tweak Y` give `feat/auth-add-x-and-tweak-y`. Then run `git checkout -b <derived-name>`.

Never wrap `git` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper — always invoke the literal command. Report the branch name you ended up on and whether you created it.

Stage the working tree changes that belong in the commit stack.

Run `git diff` and `git diff --cached` and read every hunk before staging anything. Never run a blanket `git add -A` or `git add .`.

Stage only files that are intentional source changes. Deliberately leave out generated files, build artifacts, dependency directories, editor scratch files, lockfiles you did not mean to touch, and anything that contains a credential, token, or other secret. If one file mixes intentional and unintentional changes, stage only the intended hunks (`git add -p` or an equivalent patch-mode selection).

Report the list of files you staged, and separately the list you left unstaged with a one-line reason for each exclusion. Do not create, amend, or rebase any commit in this step.

Structure the device-accurate spec as two layers, so the pixels a human reviews are the exact pixels proven against the app. PER-STATE HARNESS: one standalone page per state. Size it to the logical viewport by setting html and body to the measured logical width and height in px, with 1 CSS px = 1 dp/pt, and draw only the app's own screen content — the surface's tokens in :root taken from its design system or its theme source (or from the sampled values when it has none), the app's bundled fonts via @font-face, and every element absolutely positioned from the geometry measured in the previous stage. No OS chrome on this page. It is both what you screenshot for the diff and what the shell embeds, so the two can never drift. SPEC SHELL: a canvas with a meta-card plus a states band, which the caller supplies. Each state is a device frame whose screen embeds its harness with an <iframe>; draw the platform's status bar and home indicator cosmetically on top with pointer-events:none, and keep them out of the diff. The caller fixes the harness filenames, the iframe src values, and where the fonts live; everything else here is yours to decide.

Close out in a few lines. Give the fully qualified absolute path of the committed implementation plan — never a repo-relative path — and the number of steps it contains.

Then surface anything the developer needs to know before execution: the low-expertise or blocked-no-tooling rows from the Verification Coverage table, and, if the project has no test framework at all, the fact that one should be set up. Do not begin implementing.

The developer's answers are in context under human.gate.text.

Record the final choice for each decision, with a one-line reason tied back to the requirement or constraint that drove it. Where the developer overrode your recommendation, record their choice as the decision — do not re-argue it.

Then check whether any decision is still open: one they did not answer, or a follow-up that only became askable now that an earlier answer has landed. List those explicitly. If nothing is left open, say the decisions are settled and the plan can be drafted.

The verify step failed. Read its output in the context above and fix the stack.

Common causes and their fixes:
- A rebase is still in progress: resolve the conflicts, `git add` the resolved files, and `git rebase --continue` until it finishes. Only `git rebase --abort` if the stack cannot be salvaged, and say so explicitly in your output.

The verification failed: either the bug is still there or the fix regressed something. Diagnose further rather than patching harder.

If the symptom persists, your root cause was wrong or incomplete — go back to the trace, work out what the previous attempt missed, and state a corrected root cause. Count the fix attempts made so far against the maximum number of fix attempts, which defaults to 5 unless the caller specified another number.

End this stage as SUCCEEDED if attempts remain, and hand forward the corrected root cause and a revised fix approach for the next attempt. End this stage as FAILED if the attempt budget is exhausted — the workflow then stops and reports honestly rather than thrashing.

Push the branch. Determine which of three cases applies from a single check, then run the one matching push command:

    git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u} 2>/dev/null && echo "ahead=$(git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD) behind=$(git rev-list --count HEAD..@{u})" || echo "no-upstream"

CASE A — the check prints `no-upstream`: there is no upstream, so push and set one with `git push -u origin <branch-name>`.

CASE B — there is an upstream and `behind` is 0: the local branch fast-forwards the remote, so a plain `git push` succeeds.

CASE C — there is an upstream and both `ahead` and `behind` are greater than zero: history diverged because the commit step rewrote it, so run `git push --force-with-lease`. Invoking this workflow constitutes the developer's pre-authorization for `git push --force-with-lease` on this branch. Never use a bare `git push --force`; `--force-with-lease` refuses to push if the remote moved unexpectedly, and that safety net must be preserved.

Save the confirmed repro verbatim so later phases can re-run it exactly: the PRECONDITIONS and data, the ORDERED minimal steps, the OBSERVED (wrong) result, the EXPECTED result, and the evidence. Every verification in this workflow runs against exactly these steps, so restate them in full rather than summarizing them away.

End this stage as SUCCEEDED only if the report says the bug was reproduced and someone was observed to see the wrong behavior. End this stage as FAILED if the report is a could-not-reproduce result. Never upgrade a could-not-reproduce into a reproduction, and never invent steps the report does not contain.

Task: BUG: CLI table text is unreadable on dark terminal themes.

SYMPTOM
Secondary text in `fabro` CLI tables is hardcoded to `Color::Ansi256(8)` ("bright
black" — a fixed dark grey from the palette). That assumes a light terminal
background; on a dark theme it renders nearly invisible against the background.
Reproduced by the user with `fabro workflow list`, where the DESCRIPTION column
is unreadable.

LOCATIONS — 10 occurrences in 4 files, all under
lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/
  runs/list.rs         6  (lines 128, 138, 148, 178, 184, 185)
  model.rs             2  (lines 135, 138)
  workflow/list.rs     1  (line 113)
  run/checkpoints.rs   1  (line 93)

runs/list.rs is the worst case: line 178 uses Ansi256(8) as a *status* color and
line 184 suppresses bold for it, so a run status is conveyed entirely by a color
the user cannot see. This is not purely cosmetic.

SUSPECTED CAUSE
An absolute palette index is used where a terminal-relative attribute belongs.
The codebase already has the right primitive: `fabro_util::terminal::Styles::dim`
= `Style::new().dim()` at lib/foundation/fabro-util/src/terminal.rs:28. It emits
SGR 2 (faint) against the terminal's own foreground, so it adapts to the theme.
workflow/list.rs already uses `styles.dim` for the section path in
`print_section` — the table cells in the same file just don't.

OPEN QUESTION — resolve this before choosing the fix
Does cli-table 0.5's `CellStruct` expose a faint/dim attribute the way it exposes
`.bold(bool)`? Check the actual crate source in the cargo registry rather than
guessing. Three ways it can go:
  a) If CellStruct has a faint/dim attribute, use it. Cleanest.
  b) Otherwise pre-apply the dim style to the string before `.cell()`. Risk:
     cli-table's column width measurement may count the embedded ANSI escape
     codes and mis-align the table. Verify alignment if taking this path.
  c) As a last resort pick a mid-tone color readable on both light and dark
     backgrounds — but this still absolutizes what should be relative.

Note all styling here already goes through the `use_color` flag via
`color_if()`, so the no-color path is unaffected either way.

CONTRIBUTION PATH
Per CONTRIBUTING.md this qualifies as a "bug fix / small improvement" — send a
PR directly, no issue needed. The `origin` remote is the fork
carllelandtaylor/fabro; `upstream` is fabro-sh/fabro and its push URL is
DISABLED, so push branches to `origin` only. Branch from main and open the PR
against fabro-sh/fabro main, e.g.

  gh pr create --repo fabro-sh/fabro --base main --head carllelandtaylor:<branch>

REQUIRED CHECKS (CONTRIBUTING.md's list is stale relative to CI — use these)
  cargo nextest run --workspace
  cargo +nightly-2026-04-14 fmt --check --all
  cargo +nightly-2026-04-14 clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
The pinned nightly matters: stable rustfmt will not match CI.

VERIFICATION
No existing test covers this. Add one asserting the faint attribute (or whatever
the chosen mechanism emits) so this cannot regress. Manually verify the rendered
output against both a light and a dark terminal profile.

Create the pull request, or update the existing one in place. Start with `gh pr view --json number,url,state 2>/dev/null`.

If a PR exists and its state is OPEN, take the UPDATE path. If a PR exists and its state is MERGED, ignore it and take the CREATE path — that PR is no longer active. If a PR exists and its state is CLOSED, ask the developer whether to reopen it with `gh pr reopen <number>`, create a new one, or stop. If no PR exists, take the CREATE path.

UPDATE PATH. Never regenerate the body from scratch: the developer may have added sections, screenshots, Loom links, reviewer notes or rewordings that a wholesale replacement would destroy. Do it in a single pass — fetch once, edit once, and do not re-read afterwards to verify. Fetch the current body once with `gh pr view <number> --json title,body`, treat it as the source of truth, and apply the minimum set of edits that make it reflect the current branch state: correct stale information in place, add genuinely new information to the most appropriate existing section, and remove or revise only the specific sentences or bullets that are no longer true. Leave everything else verbatim, including developer-added sections and inline additions; when unsure whether something is stale, keep it. Treat `## Screenshots` under the same rule: if this run captured screenshots and the body has no Screenshots section, add one in the captured form; if a Screenshots section already exists, refresh only its directory pointer and file list to match the currently committed screenshots; if the change is non-visual, leave the body's Screenshots handling untouched. On the update path do NOT insert or modify any `Resolves #N` line and do NOT set a Project Status — that is handled by other automation. Apply everything with a single `gh pr edit <number> --body "..."`.

CREATE PATH. Before running `gh pr create`, check for an active Issue:

    if facto-helper.sh tracker.exists 2>/dev/null; then ISSUE_NUMBER="$(facto-helper.sh current-issue 2>/dev/null)" || ISSUE_NUMBER=""; fi

label.String: Phase 4: Capture Screenshots Of Visual Changes

prompt.String:
Capture screenshots of any visual change on this branch. This whole step is autonomous — never ask the developer, and never let a capture failure abort the PR.

FIRST, judge on your own whether the changes in this PR could plausibly affect the UI or UX that a person sees or interacts with. Reason about what the change actually does; do not rely on a checklist, a file-extension list, or any other heuristic. If the change could not affect the UI or UX, capture nothing, record that the change is non-visual, and finish this step — no Screenshots section will go into the PR body.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL, delegate the capture work to a subagent so the heavy image tokens stay out of this workflow's context; the subagent must return only the list of screenshot paths and their labels, never the images themselves. The subagent does the following.

1. Resolve the directory: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir)/screenshots"`. If `facto-helper.sh task-dir` fails because you are not in a task worktree, pass a short kebab-case slug instead: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir "<slug>")/screenshots"`. Then `mkdir -p "$SHOTS_DIR"`.
2. Remove stale screenshots from earlier runs so the directory always reflects the current app: `git rm -q "$SHOTS_DIR"/* 2>/dev/null || true`.
3. Bring up the app and capture the after-state of every distinct surface the change affects, with no cap on how many. Prefer, in this order: a project-specific run skill or documented run instructions; the built-in run and verify skills; for web UIs the Playwright tools, navigating to the running app and taking screenshots; for native mobile, booting or attaching an emulator or simulator, launching the app and navigating to the affected screens. Save each capture into `$SHOTS_DIR` under a descriptive labelled filename such as `dashboard-after.png`.
4. Best-effort before-state: when the change modifies an existing screen rather than adding a brand-new one, and the base version is cheaply runnable, add a worktree at the merge base with `git worktree add <tmp> "$(git merge-base main HEAD)"`, run that version, capture the same surfaces into `$SHOTS_DIR` as `*-before.png`, then remove the worktree with `git worktree remove <tmp> --force`. 5. Stage ONLY `$SHOTS_DIR` — never `git add -A`. The next step commits what you staged.

    git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u} 2>/dev/null && echo "ahead=$(git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD) behind=$(git rev-list --count HEAD..@{u})" || echo "no-upstream"

prompt.String: A close-looking mock is not proof. Render the mock at the device's exact pixel resolution and diff it against the live screenshot. (1) RENDER AT DSF: headless Chrome with --headless=new --force-device-scale-factor=<dsf> --window-size=<logicalW>,<logicalH> --virtual-time-budget=4000 --screenshot=mock.png <url>, or a Playwright context with a matching deviceScaleFactor. Screenshot the bare harness page for the state, not the spec shell, so the diff covers only the design, then crop to the device resolution. Because the shell embeds that same harness, the reviewed pixels and the proven pixels stay identical. (2) DIFF: compare the two same-size PNGs overall and per region or band — PIL ImageChops.difference plus histogram() works with no numpy — and also measure the left edge, right edge and width of key elements, because sub-pixel drift accumulates across a row and is hard to catch by eye. ACCEPTANCE BAR: a designer and an engineer looking at both agree they match — no visible structural, color or type mismatch in the app's own content, with the remaining diff being anti-aliasing and OS chrome. End this stage as succeeded only when the diff is under that bar; end it as failed when it is not, so the workflow revises the mock and re-renders.

prompt.String:
Review the full diff of the stack under review. Launch a subagent with `model: "opus"` to do the reviewing, so the diff and the changed files stay out of this workflow's context; instruct it to read `git diff <base>..HEAD` and every changed file in full before judging anything.

The subagent evaluates the changes against all of: CORRECTNESS — bugs, logic errors, off-by-one errors, null and undefined handling, race conditions. ERROR HANDLING — missing error cases, swallowed errors, unhelpful error messages. EDGE CASES — empty inputs, boundary values, unexpected types, concurrent access. label.String: Phase 6: Create Or Update The PR

prompt.String:
Create the pull request, or update the existing one in place. Start with `gh pr view --json number,url,state 2>/dev/null`.

If a PR exists and its state is OPEN, take the UPDATE path. If a PR exists and its state is MERGED, ignore it and take the CREATE path — that PR is no longer active. If a PR exists and its state is CLOSED, ask the developer whether to reopen it with `gh pr reopen <number>`, create a new one, or stop. If no PR exists, take the CREATE path.

UPDATE PATH. Never regenerate the body from scratch: the developer may have added sections, screenshots, Loom links, reviewer notes or rewordings that a wholesale replacement would destroy. Do it in a single pass — fetch once, edit once, and do not re-read afterwards to verify. Fetch the current body once with `gh pr view <number> --json title,body`, treat it as the source of truth, and apply the minimum set of edits that make it reflect the current branch state: correct stale information in place, add genuinely new information to the most appropriate existing section, and remove or revise only the specific sentences or bullets that are no longer true. Leave everything else verbatim, including developer-added sections and inline additions; when unsure whether something is stale, keep it. Treat `## Screenshots` under the same rule: if this run captured screenshots and the body has no Screenshots section, add one in the captured form; if a Screenshots section already exists, refresh only its directory pointer and file list to match the currently committed screenshots; if the change is non-visual, leave the body's Screenshots handling untouched. On the update path do NOT insert or modify any `Resolves #N` line and do NOT set a Project Status — that is handled by other automation. Apply everything with a single `gh pr edit <number> --body "..."`.

CREATE PATH. Before running `gh pr create`, check for an active Issue:

    if facto-helper.sh tracker.exists 2>/dev/null; then ISSUE_NUMBER="$(facto-helper.sh current-issue 2>/dev/null)" || ISSUE_NUMBER=""; fi

If `$ISSUE_NUMBER` is set, build the PR-link line by substituting `{issue}` into `facto-helper.sh tracker.field pr_link_format` — default `Resolves #{issue}`, giving `Resolves #123` — and insert it as the second line of the `## Summary` section, immediately after the one-line summary. If `tracker.exists` fails or `current-issue` returns nothing, skip the link entirely.

Build the body from the PR body template at [facto] claude/skills/pr/pr-body-template.md, which defines every section — Summary, Reason for change, What changed, Screenshots, Notable technical choices, Verification — and the footer. Keep the PR title short and in conventional commit format such as `feat:`, `fix:` or `refactor:`, under 70 characters. Fill Reason for change from the reason established earlier in this run. Fill `## Screenshots` from the outcome of the capture step: when capture succeeded use the pointer form, building the directory link from `REPO_SLUG="$(gh repo view --json nameWithOwner -q .nameWithOwner)"`, `BRANCH="$(git branch --show-current)"` and `REL="$(realpath --relative-to="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" "$SHOTS_DIR")"` into `https://github.com/$REPO_SLUG/tree/$BRANCH/$REL`, with one bullet per committed file labelled by screen or state and by before or after; when capture failed use the placeholder form, keeping the unchecked `- [ ] Attach screenshots before merging` item and quoting the specific recorded reason; when the change is non-visual omit the `## Screenshots` section entirely.

Every Manual verification step must describe something that could fail even if every file in the diff is exactly as shown — running a command, starting a dev server and exercising a path, checking a CI run's outcome, parsing a config with a real tool. Do NOT write steps that merely verify a file exists, that content is present, or that a line was deleted; the diff already proves those. `npx playwright test foo.spec.ts` is acceptable, `confirm file X exists` is not; `start dev server, click X, expect Y` is acceptable, `verify section Y is present` is not. Verification steps must be specific enough for someone unfamiliar with the change to follow them. For documentation-only, comment-only, gitignore or pure-config changes with no executable behavior, replace the numbered list with `N/A — documentation-only change; diff review is sufficient.` rather than fabricating steps. End the body with `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`.

After `gh pr create` succeeds and you have captured the PR URL, and only when `$ISSUE_NUMBER` was set, set that issue's Project Status to the tracker's `status_values.in_review` using the inline `gh project item-edit` pattern. A Status-write failure is a warning, not an error — say so and continue, because the PR itself is the deliverable.

Report whether the PR was created or updated, its number, its URL and its title.

prompt.String:
Create the pull request, or update the existing one in place. Start with `gh pr view --json number,url,state 2>/dev/null`.

If a PR exists and its state is OPEN, take the UPDATE path. If a PR exists and its state is MERGED, ignore it and take the CREATE path — that PR is no longer active. If a PR exists and its state is CLOSED, ask the developer whether to reopen it with `gh pr reopen <number>`, create a new one, or stop. If no PR exists, take the CREATE path.

UPDATE PATH. Never regenerate the body from scratch: the developer may have added sections, screenshots, Loom links, reviewer notes or rewordings that a wholesale replacement would destroy. Do it in a single pass — fetch once, edit once, and do not re-read afterwards to verify. Fetch the current body once with `gh pr view <number> --json title,body`, treat it as the source of truth, and apply the minimum set of edits that make it reflect the current branch state: correct stale information in place, add genuinely new information to the most appropriate existing section, and remove or revise only the specific sentences or bullets that are no longer true. Leave everything else verbatim, including developer-added sections and inline additions; when unsure whether something is stale, keep it. Treat `## Screenshots` under the same rule: if this run captured screenshots and the body has no Screenshots section, add one in the captured form; if a Screenshots section already exists, refresh only its directory pointer and file list to match the currently committed screenshots; if the change is non-visual, leave the body's Screenshots handling untouched. On the update path do NOT insert or modify any `Resolves #N` line and do NOT set a Project Status — that is handled by other automation. Apply everything with a single `gh pr edit <number> --body "..."`.

CREATE PATH. Before running `gh pr create`, check for an active Issue:

    if facto-helper.sh tracker.exists 2>/dev/null; then ISSUE_NUMBER="$(facto-helper.sh current-issue 2>/dev/null)" || ISSUE_NUMBER=""; fi

If `$ISSUE_NUMBER` is set, build the PR-link line by substituting `{issue}` into `facto-helper.sh tracker.field pr_link_format` — default `Resolves #{issue}`, giving `Resolves #123` — and insert it as the second line of the `## Summary` section, immediately after the one-line summary. If `tracker.exists` fails or `current-issue` returns nothing, skip the link entirely.

Build the body from the PR body template at [facto] claude/skills/pr/pr-body-template.md, which defines every section — Summary, Reason for change, What changed, Screenshots, Notable technical choices, Verification — and the footer. Keep the PR title short and in conventional commit format such as `feat:`, `fix:` or `refactor:`, under 70 characters. Fill Reason for change from the reason established earlier in this run. Fill `## Screenshots` from the outcome of the capture step: when capture succeeded use the pointer form, building the directory link from `REPO_SLUG="$(gh repo view --json nameWithOwner -q .nameWithOwner)"`, `BRANCH="$(git branch --show-current)"` and `REL="$(realpath --relative-to="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" "$SHOTS_DIR")"` into `https://github.com/$REPO_SLUG/tree/$BRANCH/$REL`, with one bullet per committed file labelled by screen or state and by before or after; when capture failed use the placeholder form, keeping the unchecked `- [ ] Attach screenshots before merging` item and quoting the specific recorded reason; when the change is non-visual omit the `## Screenshots` section entirely.

Every Manual verification step must describe something that could fail even if every file in the diff is exactly as shown — running a command, starting a dev server and exercising a path, checking a CI run's outcome, parsing a config with a real tool. Do NOT write steps that merely verify a file exists, that content is present, or that a line was deleted; the diff already proves those. `npx playwright test foo.spec.ts` is acceptable, `confirm file X exists` is not; `start dev server, click X, expect Y` is acceptable, `verify section Y is present` is not. Verification steps must be specific enough for someone unfamiliar with the change to follow them. For documentation-only, comment-only, gitignore or pure-config changes with no executable behavior, replace the numbered list with `N/A — documentation-only change; diff review is sufficient.` rather than fabricating steps. End the body with `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)`.

After `gh pr create` succeeds and you have captured the PR URL, and only when `$ISSUE_NUMBER` was set, set that issue's Project Status to the tracker's `status_values.in_review` using the inline `gh project item-edit` pattern. A Status-write failure is a warning, not an error — say so and continue, because the PR itself is the deliverable.

Report whether the PR was created or updated, its number, its URL and its title.

prompt.String:
Capture screenshots of any visual change on this branch. This whole step is autonomous — never ask the developer, and never let a capture failure abort the PR.

FIRST, judge on your own whether the changes in this PR could plausibly affect the UI or UX that a person sees or interacts with. Reason about what the change actually does; do not rely on a checklist, a file-extension list, or any other heuristic. If the change could not affect the UI or UX, capture nothing, record that the change is non-visual, and finish this step — no Screenshots section will go into the PR body.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL, delegate the capture work to a subagent so the heavy image tokens stay out of this workflow's context; the subagent must return only the list of screenshot paths and their labels, never the images themselves. The subagent does the following.

1. Resolve the directory: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir)/screenshots"`. If `facto-helper.sh task-dir` fails because you are not in a task worktree, pass a short kebab-case slug instead: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir "<slug>")/screenshots"`. Then `mkdir -p "$SHOTS_DIR"`.
2. Remove stale screenshots from earlier runs so the directory always reflects the current app: `git rm -q "$SHOTS_DIR"/* 2>/dev/null || true`.
3. Bring up the app and capture the after-state of every distinct surface the change affects, with no cap on how many. Prefer, in this order: a project-specific run skill or documented run instructions; the built-in run and verify skills; for web UIs the Playwright tools, navigating to the running app and taking screenshots; for native mobile, booting or attaching an emulator or simulator, launching the app and navigating to the affected screens. Save each capture into `$SHOTS_DIR` under a descriptive labelled filename such as `dashboard-after.png`.
4. Best-effort before-state: when the change modifies an existing screen rather than adding a brand-new one, and the base version is cheaply runnable, add a worktree at the merge base with `git worktree add <tmp> "$(git merge-base main HEAD)"`, run that version, capture the same surfaces into `$SHOTS_DIR` as `*-before.png`, then remove the worktree with `git worktree remove <tmp> --force`. For brand-new screens capture after-only. If running the base version is impractical because of an expensive rebuild or missing services, skip the before-state and note that.
5. Stage ONLY `$SHOTS_DIR` — never `git add -A`. The next step commits what you staged.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL BUT NO VIABLE WAY TO RUN THE APP AND CAPTURE EXISTS, capture nothing and record the specific reason, for example 'no emulator available' or 'app build failed'. The PR body will then carry the placeholder form of the Screenshots section quoting that reason.

Never wrap `git` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper. Report exactly one of: the committed-screenshot paths with their labels; the specific capture-failure reason; or that the change is non-visual.

Understand the bug report. The input is either a GitHub Issue number or a free-text description of the symptom: BUG: CLI table text is unreadable on dark terminal themes.

SYMPTOM
Secondary text in `fabro` CLI tables is hardcoded to `Color::Ansi256(8)` ("bright
black" — a fixed dark grey from the palette). That assumes a light terminal
background; on a dark theme it renders nearly invisible against the background.
Reproduced by the user with `fabro workflow list`, where the DESCRIPTION column
is unreadable.

LOCATIONS — 10 occurrences in 4 files, all under
lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/
  runs/list.rs         6  (lines 128, 138, 148, 178, 184, 185)
  model.rs             2  (lines 135, 138)
  workflow/list.rs     1  (line 113)
  run/checkpoints.rs   1  (line 93)

runs/list.rs is the worst case: line 178 uses Ansi256(8) as a *status* color and
line 184 suppresses bold for it, so a run status is conveyed entirely by a color
the user cannot see. This is not purely cosmetic.

SUSPECTED CAUSE
An absolute palette index is used where a terminal-relative attribute belongs.
The codebase already has the right primitive: `fabro_util::terminal::Styles::dim`
= `Style::new().dim()` at lib/foundation/fabro-util/src/terminal.rs:28. It emits
SGR 2 (faint) against the terminal's own foreground, so it adapts to the theme.
workflow/list.rs already uses `styles.dim` for the section path in
`print_section` — the table cells in the same file just don't.

Does cli-table 0.5's `CellStruct` expose a faint/dim attribute the way it exposes
`.bold(bool)`? Check the actual crate source in the cargo registry rather than
guessing. Three ways it can go:

  b) Otherwise pre-apply the dim style to the string before `.cell()`. Risk:
     cli-table's column width measurement may count the embedded ANSI escape
     codes and mis-align the table. Verify alignment if taking this path.
  c) As a last resort pick a mid-tone color readable on both light and dark
     backgrounds — but this still absolutizes what should be relative.

Note all styling here already goes through the `use_color` flag via
`color_if()`, so the no-color path is unaffected either way.

carllelandtaylor/fabro; `upstream` is fabro-sh/fabro and its push URL is

against fabro-sh/fabro main, e.g.

Push the branch. Determine which of three cases applies from a single check, then run the one matching push command:

    git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u} 2>/dev/null && echo "ahead=$(git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD) behind=$(git rev-list --count HEAD..@{u})" || echo "no-upstream"

CASE A — the check prints `no-upstream`: there is no upstream, so push and set one with `git push -u origin <branch-name>`.

CASE B — there is an upstream and `behind` is 0: the local branch fast-forwards the remote, so a plain `git push` succeeds.

CASE C — there is an upstream and both `ahead` and `behind` are greater than zero: history diverged because the commit step rewrote it, so run `git push --force-with-lease`. Invoking this workflow constitutes the developer's pre-authorization for `git push --force-with-lease` on this branch. Never use a bare `git push --force`; `--force-with-lease` refuses to push if the remote moved unexpectedly, and that safety net must be preserved.

Never wrap `git push` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper — that trips bypass detection and hardens the classifier for the whole session. Always invoke the literal command. Report which case applied and the push result.

Compare the implementation against the mock, dimension by dimension, with evidence. Launch a dedicated comparison subagent per screen, or batched across screens, using an opus-class model. The PR body must state why this change is being made, so establish that reason now. Do not ask the developer yet.

First try to derive the reason from what you already have: the goal and context given to this run, any requirements, product requirements documents, design documents or ticket links supplied by the caller, and the Context lines in the bodies of the commits ahead of main (`git log main..HEAD --format=%B`). Also read the diff itself for evidence of the problem being solved. A good reason names the user-facing problem being solved, the technical problem or limitation being addressed, the opportunity being taken, or the strategic decision behind the change — and is specific about the before and after where that is relevant.

End this stage as SUCCEEDED and state the reason in one short paragraph if you can establish it from that evidence. End this stage as FAILED if the evidence genuinely does not tell you why the change is being made — the next step will ask the developer directly. Do not invent a reason to avoid failing.

Otherwise report, in this order:

4. The final commit stack as `git log <base>..HEAD --oneline` printed it.

The verify step failed. Read its output in the context above and fix the stack.

prompt.String:
Capture screenshots of any visual change on this branch. This whole step is autonomous — never ask the developer, and never let a capture failure abort the PR.

FIRST, judge on your own whether the changes in this PR could plausibly affect the UI or UX that a person sees or interacts with. Reason about what the change actually does; do not rely on a checklist, a file-extension list, or any other heuristic. If the change could not affect the UI or UX, capture nothing, record that the change is non-visual, and finish this step — no Screenshots section will go into the PR body.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL, delegate the capture work to a subagent so the heavy image tokens stay out of this workflow's context; the subagent must return only the list of screenshot paths and their labels, never the images themselves. The subagent does the following.

1. Resolve the directory: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir)/screenshots"`. If `facto-helper.sh task-dir` fails because you are not in a task worktree, pass a short kebab-case slug instead: `SHOTS_DIR="$(facto-helper.sh task-dir "<slug>")/screenshots"`. Then `mkdir -p "$SHOTS_DIR"`.
2. Remove stale screenshots from earlier runs so the directory always reflects the current app: `git rm -q "$SHOTS_DIR"/* 2>/dev/null || true`.
3. Bring up the app and capture the after-state of every distinct surface the change affects, with no cap on how many. Prefer, in this order: a project-specific run skill or documented run instructions; the built-in run and verify skills; for web UIs the Playwright tools, navigating to the running app and taking screenshots; for native mobile, booting or attaching an emulator or simulator, launching the app and navigating to the affected screens. Save each capture into `$SHOTS_DIR` under a descriptive labelled filename such as `dashboard-after.png`.
4. Best-effort before-state: when the change modifies an existing screen rather than adding a brand-new one, and the base version is cheaply runnable, add a worktree at the merge base with `git worktree add <tmp> "$(git merge-base main HEAD)"`, run that version, capture the same surfaces into `$SHOTS_DIR` as `*-before.png`, then remove the worktree with `git worktree remove <tmp> --force`. For brand-new screens capture after-only. If running the base version is impractical because of an expensive rebuild or missing services, skip the before-state and note that.
5. Stage ONLY `$SHOTS_DIR` — never `git add -A`. The next step commits what you staged.

IF THE CHANGE IS VISUAL BUT NO VIABLE WAY TO RUN THE APP AND CAPTURE EXISTS, capture nothing and record the specific reason, for example 'no emulator available' or 'app build failed'. The PR body will then carry the placeholder form of the Screenshots section quoting that reason.

Never wrap `git` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper. Report exactly one of: the committed-screenshot paths with their labels; the specific capture-failure reason; or that the change is non-visual.

label.String: Phase 4: Capture Screenshots Of Visual Changes

Write a per-screen checklist that tells the developer exactly what to eyeball against the design mock: for each in-scope screen and state, the mock frame it corresponds to, and the concrete things to check on it — layout and element order, spacing and sizing, colors and theme tokens, typography, icons and imagery, exact copy, and the component states the mock draws. label.String: Phase 3 — Answer the decisions in one go: which option you want for each, and where my recommendation is wrong. Add any constraint I should be honouring that I haven't.

prompt.String:
Break the developer's feedback into discrete changes. Each change must be self-contained — a single edit that can be described in one sentence, such as 'remove plan.md from the repo', 'rename `fetchData` to `loadData`', or 'add error handling to the webhook endpoint'.

For each change, state what to change, where it lives, and what the result should look like. Then note the dependencies between them: which changes touch the same files, and which ones depend on another change's result. That determines whether the work runs in parallel or in sequence.

End this stage as SUCCEEDED and output the numbered list of discrete changes when the feedback is clear enough to act on. End this stage as FAILED when any part of the feedback is unclear or ambiguous — when you cannot tell which file, symbol or behavior is meant, or when a request could reasonably be read two different ways — and say precisely what is ambiguous and what you need to know. The next step asks the developer, and their answer comes back here to be parsed again. Do not guess at ambiguous feedback in order to avoid failing.

Stage the working tree changes that belong in the commit stack.

Run `git diff` and `git diff --cached` and read every hunk before staging anything. Never run a blanket `git add -A` or `git add .`.

Stage only files that are intentional source changes. Deliberately leave out generated files, build artifacts, dependency directories, editor scratch files, lockfiles you did not mean to touch, and anything that contains a credential, token, or other secret. If one file mixes intentional and unintentional changes, stage only the intended hunks (`git add -p` or an equivalent patch-mode selection).

Report the list of files you staged, and separately the list you left unstaged with a one-line reason for each exclusion. Do not create, amend, or rebase any commit in this step.

Report what this run did, using only what actually happened in the steps above. Do not invent commits.

If the assess step reported a clean working tree, say `Nothing to commit` and stop there.

Otherwise report, in this order:
1. Which files were amended into which existing commits, naming each target commit by hash and subject.
2. Which new commits were created, with their subject lines.
3. Which files were deliberately left unstaged, and why.
4. The final commit stack as `git log <base>..HEAD --oneline` printed it.
5. Anything the repair step had to fix, and anything still unresolved.

script.String: set +e; echo '--- branch ---'; git branch --show-current; echo '--- log (main..HEAD) ---'; git log main..HEAD --oneline; echo '--- diffstat (main...HEAD) ---'; git diff main...HEAD --stat; echo '--- status ---'; git status --porcelain; git diff @{u}..HEAD --quiet 2>/dev/null; UP=$?; echo "remote_uptodate=$UP"; AHEAD=$(git rev-list main..HEAD --count 2>/dev/null); [ -n "$AHEAD" ] || AHEAD=0; echo "ahead=$AHEAD"; echo '--- upstream ---'; git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u} 2>/dev/null || echo 'no-upstream'; echo '--- existing pr ---'; gh pr view --json number,url,state,title 2>/dev/null || echo 'no-pr'; if [ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ] && { [ "$AHEAD" = "0" ] || [ "$UP" = "0" ]; }; then echo 'NOTHING TO PR: working tree is clean and there is nothing new to push'; exit 1; fi; echo 'OK: there is something to put in a PR'

prompt.String: Inspect the screenshots for anything that looks broken or visually wrong. Launch a subagent with an opus-class model and give it the screenshots. Instruct it to flag layout problems, clipped or overflowing content, misaligned elements, missing content, obvious rendering errors, and anything else that would read as a bug to a user. There is no reference to compare against, so the bar is simply whether the screen looks intentional and working. Have it report per screen, naming the specific defect and where on the screen it appears, and saying explicitly when a screen has no issues rather than staying silent about it. Collect the results into one list of findings for the report.

Report the outcome of the review loop, using only what actually happened in the steps above. Do not invent findings, fixes, or cycles.

Report, in this order: HOW MANY CYCLES were run. WHAT WAS ADDRESSED in each cycle, as a brief list per cycle. ANYTHING LEFT UNADDRESSED or committed without review, and why — in particular the minors that were deliberately skipped on a terminal cycle, and any critical or important findings still outstanding because the cycle cap was reached. HOW THE LOOP ENDED: on a clean cycle with no in-scope findings, on an all-minor terminal cycle, or on the cycle cap. OUT-OF-SCOPE OBSERVATIONS — every issue the review noticed that falls outside the scope of the current changes, stated clearly enough that the developer can act on them separately if they choose; these were noted and never fixed, by design. WHETHER AN EXISTING PR WAS UPDATED, with its URL, or that no PR existed to update — a new PR is never created by this loop.

Run the plan's final validation, now that every step is implemented.

Locate the plan's Verification or Test Plan section and RE-READ IT VERBATIM. Execute every checkbox in it, in order. Do not substitute a different test plan derived from memory or from your own summary of the plan — the plan's text is authoritative.

That normally means the full test suite, the linter, the type checker, the build, and any end-to-end or manual verification steps the plan names. Run each one and read its output.

If something fails, first search the plan for a documented fallback for the failing area with `grep -i -E 'fallback|if this fails|alternative|in case of failure' <path-to-plan-file>`, substituting the actual plan file path, and check for a Fallback sub-section co-located with that verification step. Attempt any documented fallback before treating the failure as unresolved.

End this stage as SUCCEEDED when every verification step in the plan's Test Plan section passes, or when the only remaining failures have been through the fix stage twice already — in that case say so explicitly. End this stage as FAILED when something fails and has not yet been through a fix attempt, quoting the failing command and its error output. Either way, enumerate every verification step from the plan with its outcome: ran and passed, ran and failed, skipped, or deferred with a reason.

Apply the attribution decided in the previous step. Process the groups strictly in this order: earlier commits first, then the most recent commit, then net-new.

EARLIER-COMMIT CHANGES
    git add <files>
    git commit --fixup=<target-commit-hash>
Create every fixup commit first. When they all exist, squash them in a single pass:
    GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true git rebase -i --autosquash <base>
If the rebase stops on a conflict, resolve it, `git add` the resolved files, and `git rebase --continue`. Never leave a rebase in progress.

MOST-RECENT-COMMIT CHANGES
    git add <files>
    git commit --amend --no-edit

NET-NEW CHANGES
    git add <files>
    git commit -m <message>

Commit message rules for every new commit. Subject line: imperative mood, no trailing period, describing what the change does. The body must include a Context line saying why this change exists — and when the change introduces a new library, API, or service, what it is and why it was chosen. Add a Verification section when it is meaningful, split into an `Automated:` part listing the exact commands and a `Manual:` part with numbered steps and their expected results. Omit the Verification section entirely for changes that are trivially correct: documentation, comments, or config with no behavioral effect. Keep each body to 2-5 lines — enough for a developer reading `git log` to understand the change without opening the diff. Use the commit message the caller supplied if there is one; otherwise write it yourself.

Report what this run actually did, using only what happened in the stages above. Do not invent a PR, a commit, a URL or a verification you did not perform.

If the bug could not be reproduced, report that result and stop there — what was reported, everything that was tried, and why no fix was attempted.

If the fix attempts were exhausted without a clean verification, say so plainly: the attempts made, what each one tried, and the state the branch is left in. Do not present an unverified fix as done.

Otherwise report, in this order: BUG — what was reported. ROOT CAUSE — the one-line statement. PATH TAKEN — direct or escalated, and which checklist item drove it. VERIFICATION — the outcome against the logged reproduction steps, that the bug is gone and nothing regressed, and the regression test that was added, or that the project has no test suite. CI RESULT — green, or stuck with the specific failing checks and why. PR URL.

Review the full diff of the stack under review. Launch a subagent with `model: "opus"` to do the reviewing, so the diff and the changed files stay out of this workflow's context; instruct it to read `git diff <base>..HEAD` and every changed file in full before judging anything.

The subagent evaluates the changes against all of: CORRECTNESS — bugs, logic errors, off-by-one errors, null and undefined handling, race conditions. REQUIREMENTS — does the code actually achieve what the requirements and goals specify? PROJECT CONVENTIONS — naming, patterns, file organization, and style consistency with the existing codebase. ERROR HANDLING — missing error cases, swallowed errors, unhelpful error messages. EDGE CASES — empty inputs, boundary values, unexpected types, concurrent access. SECURITY — injection, authorization gaps, secrets committed in code, and the OWASP top 10. PERFORMANCE — obvious inefficiencies such as N+1 queries, unnecessary re-renders, unbounded loops. TESTS — are new and changed behaviors covered, and do the tests actually test the right thing?

The subagent must scope its feedback to the changes under review and sort every item into exactly one of two lists. IN-SCOPE: issues directly related to the changes being reviewed — bugs in new or modified code, requirements gaps in new or modified code, style issues in new or modified code. OUT-OF-SCOPE: pre-existing problems, improvements to unchanged code, and consistency issues in files that are not being modified; these are still noted but will NOT be fixed.

Every item in either list carries: FILE AND LOCATION — where the issue is; ISSUE — what is wrong; SUGGESTION — how to fix it; SEVERITY — critical, important, or minor. Severity must be assigned deliberately rather than as a formality, because severity is what decides whether another review cycle runs.

Report both lists in full, and state which cycle number this is against the cycle cap.

prompt.String:
Decide where each change belongs. Do not commit anything in this step.

The base ref and the current commit stack were printed by the assess step. For every changed file — and for every hunk separately when a single file carries changes belonging to different commits — pick exactly one destination:

1. MOST RECENT COMMIT: the change extends or fixes work done in HEAD.
2. AN EARLIER COMMIT: the change extends or fixes work done in a specific prior commit in the stack. Record that commit's hash.
3. NET-NEW: the change is unrelated to every existing commit in the stack and needs its own new commit.

Gather evidence before deciding. Run `git log <base>..HEAD -- <file>` for each changed file, and read the existing commit messages and their diffs (`git show <hash>`). Attribute on what the commits actually did, not on filename similarity.

Output an explicit attribution table: file (or hunk) -> destination -> the evidence that justifies it. Group the net-new changes and note, for each group, whether it should be one commit or several.

Stage the working tree changes that belong in the commit stack.

Run `git diff` and `git diff --cached` and read every hunk before staging anything. Never run a blanket `git add -A` or `git add .`.

Stage only files that are intentional source changes. Deliberately leave out generated files, build artifacts, dependency directories, editor scratch files, lockfiles you did not mean to touch, and anything that contains a credential, token, or other secret. If one file mixes intentional and unintentional changes, stage only the intended hunks (`git add -p` or an equivalent patch-mode selection).

Report the list of files you staged, and separately the list you left unstaged with a one-line reason for each exclusion. Do not create, amend, or rebase any commit in this step.

Push the branch. Determine which of three cases applies from a single check, then run the one matching push command:

    git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name @{u} 2>/dev/null && echo "ahead=$(git rev-list --count @{u}..HEAD) behind=$(git rev-list --count HEAD..@{u})" || echo "no-upstream"

CASE A — the check prints `no-upstream`: there is no upstream, so push and set one with `git push -u origin <branch-name>`.

CASE B — there is an upstream and `behind` is 0: the local branch fast-forwards the remote, so a plain `git push` succeeds.

CASE C — there is an upstream and both `ahead` and `behind` are greater than zero: history diverged because the commit step rewrote it, so run `git push --force-with-lease`. Invoking this workflow constitutes the developer's pre-authorization for `git push --force-with-lease` on this branch. Never use a bare `git push --force`; `--force-with-lease` refuses to push if the remote moved unexpectedly, and that safety net must be preserved.

Never wrap `git push` in `bash -c '...'` or any other shell wrapper — that trips bypass detection and hardens the classifier for the whole session. Always invoke the literal command. Report which case applied and the push result.

goal.String:
BUG: CLI table text is unreadable on dark terminal themes.

SYMPTOM
Secondary text in `fabro` CLI tables is hardcoded to `Color::Ansi256(8)` ("bright
black" — a fixed dark grey from the palette). That assumes a light terminal
background; on a dark theme it renders nearly invisible against the background.
Reproduced by the user with `fabro workflow list`, where the DESCRIPTION column
is unreadable.

LOCATIONS — 10 occurrences in 4 files, all under
lib/apps/fabro-cli/src/commands/
  runs/list.rs         6  (lines 128, 138, 148, 178, 184, 185)
  model.rs             2  (lines 135, 138)
  workflow/list.rs     1  (line 113)
  run/checkpoints.rs   1  (line 93)

runs/list.rs is the worst case: line 178 uses Ansi256(8) as a *status* color and
line 184 suppresses bold for it, so a run status is conveyed entirely by a color
the user cannot see. This is not purely cosmetic.

SUSPECTED CAUSE
An absolute palette index is used where a terminal-relative attribute belongs.
The codebase already has the right primitive: `fabro_util::terminal::Styles::dim`
= `Style::new().dim()` at lib/foundation/fabro-util/src/terminal.rs:28. It emits
SGR 2 (faint) against the terminal's own foreground, so it adapts to the theme.
workflow/list.rs already uses `styles.dim` for the section path in
`print_section` — the table cells in the same file just don't.

OPEN QUESTION — resolve this before choosing the fix
Does cli-table 0.5's `CellStruct` expose a faint/dim attribute the way it exposes
`.bold(bool)`? Check the actual crate source in the cargo registry rather than
guessing. Three ways it can go:
  a) If CellStruct has a faint/dim attribute, use it. Cleanest.
  b) Otherwise pre-apply the dim style to the string before `.cell()`. Risk:
     cli-table's column width measurement may count the embedded ANSI escape
     codes and mis-align the table. Verify alignment if taking this path.
  c) As a last resort pick a mid-tone color readable on both light and dark
     backgrounds — but this still absolutizes what should be relative.

Note all styling here already goes through the `use_color` flag via
`color_if()`, so the no-color path is unaffected either way.

CONTRIBUTION PATH
Per CONTRIBUTING.md this qualifies as a "bug fix / small improvement" — send a
PR directly, no issue needed. The `origin` remote is the fork
carllelandtaylor/fabro; `upstream` is fabro-sh/fabro and its push URL is
DISABLED, so push branches to `origin` only. Branch from main and open the PR
against fabro-sh/fabro main, e.g.

  gh pr create --repo fabro-sh/fabro --base main --head carllelandtaylor:<branch>

REQUIRED CHECKS (CONTRIBUTING.md's list is stale relative to CI — use these)
  cargo nextest run --workspace
  cargo +nightly-2026-04-14 fmt --check --all
  cargo +nightly-2026-04-14 clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
The pinned nightly matters: stable rustfmt will not match CI.

VERIFICATION
No existing test covers this. Add one asserting the faint attribute (or whatever
the chosen mechanism emits) so this cannot regress. Manually verify the rendered
output against both a light and a dark terminal profile.

digraph FactoFixBug {
    graph [goal="Fix a reported bug end-to-end and autonomously: reproduce it, diagnose the real root cause, fix it with adaptive escalation, verify against the logged repro steps, open a pull request, and drive CI to green"]
    rankdir=LR

    start [type="start", shape=Mdiamond, label="Start"]
    exit  [type="exit", shape=Msquare, label="Exit"]

    understand_locate [
        backend="acp",
        acp.command="claude-agent-acp",
        type="agent",
        label="Phase 1: Understand And Locate",
        thread_id="fix-bug",
        fidelity="full",
        prompt="Understand the bug and locate the code it lives in. The input is either a GitHub Issue number or a free-text description of the symptom: {{ goal }}.\n\nREAD THE BUG. If you were given an issue number, read it with `gh issue view <n>` and again with `gh issue view <n> --comments`; otherwise use the free-text description you were given. Capture EXPECTED BEHAVIOR versus ACTUAL BEHAVIOR, and the AFFECTED AREA — which screen, command, endpoint or module is involved.\n\nLOCATE THE CODE. Search the codebase by feature name, route, error string, command or UI label, and trace the relevant code until you understand where the behavior actually lives. Do not form a theory of the cause yet — that is a later phase — but do know which files and functions are in play.\n\nOPTIONAL STATUS WRITE, best-effort, warn and continue. If the repo has an active Issue tracker, set the Issue's Project Status to in-progress, but only when it is currently sitting at the tracker's backlog value. Use `facto-helper.sh tracker.exists` to detect the tracker and `facto-helper.sh current-issue` to get the issue number; read `project.owner`, `project.number`, `project.name`, `status_field`, `status_values.backlog`, `status_values.in_progress` and `repo` with `facto-helper.sh tracker.field <name>`; read the current status from `gh issue view <n> --repo <slug> --json projectItems`; and if it equals the backlog name, resolve the project id, status field id, option id and item id with `gh project view`, `gh project field-list` and `gh project item-list`, then apply it with `gh project item-edit`. A failure here is a warning, never an error — print the warning and carry on.\n\nCORE GUARDRAILS that govern this whole run and every phase after it. Fix the ROOT CAUSE, not the symptom — never swallow an error or special-case the one input from the report. Do NOT remove, disable or weaken working functionality to make the symptom go away; no regressions. Add a regression test that fails before the fix and passes after, wherever the project has a test suite. Work AUTONOMOUSLY — escalation in this workflow means heavier tooling for a bigger change, never a request for developer review, and the only genuinely blocking case is being unable to reproduce the bug.\n\nReport the expected-versus-actual summary, the affected area, the files and functions you traced, and the outcome of the optional Status write."
    ]

        label="Phase 2: Confirm The Reproduction",

        backend="acp",
        acp.command="claude-agent-acp",
        type="agent",
        label="Could Not Reproduce",
        prompt="The bug could not be reproduced, so this run stops here rather than attempting a speculative fix for a bug nobody has observed.         acp.command="claude-agent-acp",
        type="agent",
        label="Phase 3: Diagnose Root Cause",
        thread_id="fix-bug",
        fidelity="full",
        prompt="Trace from the reproduced symptom to the ACTUAL cause in the code — not the surface location where it manifests. Follow the data and control flow backwards from the point where the wrong behavior becomes observable until you reach the code that is genuinely wrong, and confirm your theory against the code rather than asserting it. Add instrumentation or a scratch script if that is what it takes to see the real state at the failure point.\n\nProduce exactly two things, because they drive every later phase:\n\n1. A one-line ROOT-CAUSE STATEMENT naming the specific code and the specific wrongness — for example 'the retry wrapper resets the backoff counter on every call because it is constructed inside the loop body'.\n\n2. A short PROPOSED FIX APPROACH: what should change, in which files, and why that fixes the cause rather than hiding the symptom.         backend="acp",
        acp.command="claude-agent-acp",
        type="agent",
        label="Phase 4: Choose The Fix Path",
        prompt="Choose between the direct path and the escalated path for the fix approach you just proposed.         type="conditional",
        shape=diamond,
        label="Escalated: large or structural change"

        type="conditional",
        shape=diamond,
        label="Direct: small and localized fix"

        acp.command="ANTHROPIC_MODEL=sonnet claude-agent-acp",
        type="agent",
